summary: For ages 8–9, learners build evidence-backed arguments about weather-hazard design: identify a hazard (flood, high wind, extreme sun/heat), compare at least two design solutions against shared criteria (cost, protection, feasibility), generate evidence by testing, then make a claim backed by evidence and reasoning. The emphasis is Claim + Evidence + Reasoning, not just building. Core honesty: humans cannot eliminate a natural hazard, only reduce its impacts. The central activity is a design-test-argue cycle with an A/B comparison; defending the claim to a skeptical interlocutor is a strong follow-on best used after data exists. Knowledge-check and labelled-diagram tasks are useful scaffolds for naming solutions but do not, on their own, exercise the generate-evidence-then-argue practice. For any shade/sun defence, judge it by the shadow or shaded patch cast on the ground, never by looking toward the sun.
misconceptions: Engineers can stop or prevent the hazard itself — solutions reduce IMPACTS, not the hazard
The most expensive or most complex solution is automatically best — merit depends on criteria and evidence
A claim is just an opinion — a scientific claim must be backed by evidence about criteria and constraints
One design must be perfect — real solutions involve trade-offs (cost vs protection)
If it worked once it always works — testing against the actual hazard conditions matters

activities.title: Hazard-defence test bench: run the same storm against two designs
steps: Choose a threatened place — for example a river town facing floods — and pick defences within a budget (raise the houses, build a flood barrier, widen the channel), each with a cost.

Run the hazard that your chosen defences are meant to address (e.g. a rising flood for flood defences, or a high wind for wind defences) and observe outcomes: which homes flood or are damaged and which stay protected.
Read a readout tallying damage and cost for your chosen design.
Run the SAME hazard against a second, different design and record its damage and cost so the two can be compared fairly under matched conditions.
Fill in a simple criteria/constraints table (protection level, cost, feasibility) for both designs.

State a claim naming which design is better and the evidence that supports it — for example (an illustration only; actual values depend on your test setup) 'raising the houses is the better solution because the data show less damage for a lower cost.'
Note explicitly that no design stopped the hazard — the flood or wind still happened; the designs only reduced its impact.

If you test an extreme-heat scenario instead (e.g. shading a play area), judge a shade or cover by the shadow or shaded patch it casts on the ground over time — never by looking toward the sun through or past the cover — and treat the result as the outcome of a fair comparison, not instant cooling.
activities.insight: Merit is judged by evidence against shared criteria, not by preference, expense, or complexity. Testing two designs against the identical hazard turns 'which is best' into a claim you can support with data, and shows that solutions reduce impacts rather than eliminate the hazard.

activities.title: Defend your claim to a skeptical council
steps: After you have test data, present your chosen solution to a skeptical town-council member or engineer.
Respond when they probe: 'Why is yours better than the barrier? What evidence shows it?'
Address the competing solution directly, naming its strength and why your design still wins on the criteria.
Say what evidence, if it were different, would change your mind and make the other design better.
activities.insight: A scientific claim must be defensible with reasons and evidence about criteria and constraints, and must reckon honestly with the strongest competing alternative — not just restate a preference.

activities.title: Name the hazard and its defences (scaffold)
steps: Look at a labelled building or place and reveal its defences one at a time (raised floor, flood barrier, wind-resistant roof, lightning rod, shade or insulation against extreme sun/heat).
For each defence, say what hazard it targets and what harm it is meant to reduce.
Match each hazard to one or more solutions, and describe in your own words how each solution reduces harm.

If exploring a shade or sun defence, plan to judge its effect by looking at the shadow or shaded patch it casts on the ground, and, if testing, by comparing measured temperatures of shaded and unshaded spots over time — never by looking toward the sun or holding material up to your eyes toward the sun.
activities.insight: Before arguing which design is best, learners need to know what the candidate solutions are and which harm each addresses.

checkQuestion: Give the child two or three designs meant to reduce the same weather hazard (e.g. ways to stop a building flooding, or to protect a play area from strong sun or wind). Ask them to pick which design would work best and build an argument for it using evidence — then watch how they justify the choice. Set the task and observe the claim-evidence-reasoning; don't ask them to define 'hazard.'
checkAnswer: Makes a clear claim for one design, backs it with relevant evidence about how the hazard causes harm and how the design's features reduce that harm (e.g. a raised floor keeps floodwater out; a barrier redirects wind), reasons from evidence rather than preference, and can weigh a trade-off or a competing design.
